speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
maintopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is the third time that I have had the privilege of tabling the Main Estimates before this House. Those that I am presenting today for the 1993-94 fiscal year detail the government's spending plans arising from the economic and fiscal statement made by the Minister of Finance before this House on December 2, 1992.
That statement announced certain initiatives to stimulate growth and employment, to rebuild the confidence of Canadians and to help them adjust to the new economic realities. At the same time, it sought to contain the deficit and I believe that we are clearly on target on all these points.
In keeping with our past efforts, the measures announced in the statement sought to stimulate economic growth and improve the standard of living of Canadians. They include a sound monetary and fiscal policy, an adaptation to the globalization of markets, a streamlining and renewal of the public sector, building on the strengths of Canadians and stimulating the spirit of enterprise and initiative in the private sector to sustain our economic progress.
In response to the statement, we are introducing a series of initiatives to invest in growth, invest in people, broaden trade opportunities and enhance competitiveness. For instance, we launched a Small Business Employment and Investment Package, we maintained research and development funds at their present level, despite our financial situation and we reallocated resources to focus on strategic investments for such things as highways, bridges and technology infrastructure and, of course, to optimize the results of those investments.
Along with these commitments, severe spending cuts had to be made to contain the deficit.
The major spending reduction program announced on December 2, 1992 will have an impact on the cost of programs delivered directly by the federal government on transfers to individuals and on grants and contributions to organizations and companies.
As everyone knows, the world economy has proven weaker than expected and the projections of growth for most countries have had to be revised downward.
In most OECD countries, governments have responded by implementing strict spending reductions. This was certainly the case in the United States, the United Kingdom, Italy and Sweden.
In the United Kingdom, for example, the recent announcement of a full-scale program review follows on the heels of the pre-Christmas announcement of major cuts in operating expenditures.

In keeping with the economic and fiscal statement of December 2, federal government operating expenditures including defence spending have had to be cut in relation to the February 1992 budget projections by $1 billion in 1993-94 and by $1.7 billion in 1994-95. Since personnel related spending represents two-thirds of the operating costs of the federal government, we have acted to reduce the total payroll.
As we announced, the wage restraint policy introduced in 1991 will be extended for an additional two years for all sectors of the federal government. This applies to the Prime Minister, cabinet ministers and members of Parliament among others. We are well aware of the heavy sacrifices that we have asked of our employees by freezing their salaries.
The government has also been forced to reduce other elements of departmental and agency operating budgets. As announced in the economic statement of December 2, these budgets will be reduced a further 3 per cent in 1993-94 in addition to the numerous cuts already imposed since 1984-85.
February 25, 1993

Routine Proceedings

Nevertheless, the reductions in the cost of programs delivered directly by the federal government were not going to be enough. Reductions were also necessary in transfer payments. Among other measures, the December statement announced that grants and contributions to most organizations and special interest groups would be cut by an average of 10 per cent from the levels forecast in the February 1992 budget. I am pleased to say that Old Age Security, the Guaranteed Income Supplement, Spouses' Allowances, programs for people with disabilities, War Veterans' Allowances, Veterans' Disability Pensions and major transfer payments to the provinces will not be affected by this reduction. There will be no reduction in the famine relief that Canada provides around the world.
After taking into account the cost of initiatives to stimulate growth, program spending reductions in 1993-94 will result in net savings of some $2.2 billion. These actions will ensure a significant reduction in the structural component of the deficit and will bring the deficit down to $32.6 billion in 1993-94.

Moreover, the 1993-94 main estimates show clearly that spending will be kept within the limits set in the Spending Control Act. Budgetary expenditures will increase by only 1.5 per cent in 1993-94, one of the lowest rates of growth in three decades. In fact, we have significantly reduced this rate of growth.
In 1984, program expenditure represented some 19.5 per cent of our gross domestic product. In 1993-94 it will fall to about 16.8 per cent.
There are indications that the Canadian economy is recovering and a gradual improvement in economic activity is expected throughout the year. Prime interest rates have fallen significantly in the last three months. Canada's inflation rate in 1992 was the lowest among the G-7 countries. Although too many Canadians are still unemployed, the employment situation has been improving almost continuously since last April. In fact, more than 146,000 new jobs have been created since then.
Retail sales have been rising for almost a year and our volume of exports is increasing. The OECD predicts that Canada will experience the highest rate of growth of the G-7 countries over the next two years.
Since 1984 we have pursued an ambitious strategy of expenditure management to regain control of our national finances. Our strategy is firmly in place and the results have been positive.
Our first step was to get rid of waste and inefficiency. We then moved to eliminate activities and organizations that no longer served a social purpose and we concentrated on improving the management of the federal government.
The Public Service 2000 initiative launched by the Prime Minister in 1989 has changed the Public Service significantly. The Public Service is increasingly results-o-riented and more responsive to the needs of taxpayers.
The budget tabled by the Minister of Finance in February 1992 announced other measures to provide more efficient delivery of services to Canadians.

The introduction of operating budgets in 1993-94 is perhaps the most important example of our new cost-effective way of doing business. Funds for salaries, operations, maintenance and minor capital expenses will be combined into a single operating budget for each federal department or agency. Departments will have greater flexibility in improving their efficiency and adapting their services to the changing needs of their clients.
I will conclude by repeating that our government remains firmly committed to sound management of public finances and to a comprehensive renewal of the federal Public Service. The action plan presented by the Minister of Finance last December supports economic recovery and proposes responsible ways of achieving that goal.

The Main Estimates that I am tabling today provide detailed information on how the government plans to spend $160.7 billion in 1993-94, in keeping with the economic and fiscal statement of December 2, 1992. In tabling the Main Estimates, the government is seeking authority from Parliament to spend $48.9 billion. As we know, the remaining expenditures are covered by legislative authorities previously granted by Parliament.

February 25, 1993
Routine Proceedings
My colleague, the Minister of Finance, intends to table a borrowing authority bill for 1993-94 when the House resumes sitting.
Madam Speaker, I thank you and this House for your attention.

maintopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians must have been surprised when the President of the Treasury Board made his presentation this morning, without so much as a single reference to the fact that we need to know how the operations of the Government of Canada will be managed on the revenue side. We have not had a budget since February 1992, and we have now been told that it will be the end of April or some time in May before we know exactly how the government intends to budget for its operations during the coming year.

I wonder how Canadians can be reassured, as the minister suggested they should be, by the approach the government is taking.
The government likes to pride itself on being a good manager. It has talked about responsibility and coming clean with the Canadian people. How many chief executive officers of companies could come before their shareholders and say: "We are going to spend $160 billion, but we are not going to tell you how we are going to budget for that. We are going to show you our expenditure plan but we are not going to deal with the revenue side of the equation".
This entire document is based on the economic and fiscal statement that was delivered in the House by the Minister of Finance in December of last year. This is a document that generally speaking was not very favourably received by Canadians faced with a long recession, the longest we have experienced in this country in terms of depth and duration since the 1930s.
It is going to be a tremendous problem for Canadians from all walks of life to try to plan their year's activities. We will now have a situation where Canadians will have to decide whether the economic policy is the economic
policy of the minister of defence, the economic policy of the minister of external trade or the financial policy and the tax policy of the Minister of Communications. As the Titanic seeks a new captain, there is going to be a lot of shuffling of the deck chairs as we go through the next three months as the Conservative Party tries to get a grip on where it is going.
The unusual circumstance we are faced with is a government that is going to ask Canadians to take them on faith as it is going to spend $60 billion. Today, the government is able to come to the House with documents from the minister of external trade. There are 4,300 pages I am told in the documents that the minister tabled dealing with the North American free trade agreement between Canada, the United States and Mexico.
The President of the Treasury Board came before the House with some 90 documents such as this dealing with estimates and yet, with all the apparatus of government available to it, both in finance and in national revenue, this government has not seen fit to bring a budget before the people of Canada in the fifth year of its mandate. As it struggles along toward the end of its constitutional capacity to govern this country, it is not prepared to come to the Canadian people, not with statements, but with a full-fledged budget.
I always like to attempt to give credit where credit is due. Over the years the precedent was set that this government brought in a budget at an appropriate time, usually from mid to the end of February. It brought in estimates subsequent to the presentation of the budget so that Canadians as well as parliamentarians could deal in a substantive way with what the government had planned for at least the coming year.
It may be politically expedient because of the change in the leadership of the government to delay a budget, but it is not very satisfactory for Canadians to have to struggle along based on a budget that was put together at least two years ago, at least the beginnings of it were, a budget that was based on projections, conclusions and assumptions that in many respects now are quite a way off base.
February 25, 1993

Routine Proceedings
I hope that members on both sides of the House will deal with the issues in the estimates as they are referred to committee. Surely the government has a responsibility to review its decision to delay the budget process for another two or three months.
The work that has gone into the preparation of the estimates has certainly put a clear picture before the bureaucrats and the political leaders of what they intend to do with the spending of the Canadian taxpayers' money. What is the purpose of all of this? We understand that in some of the programs, for statutory reasons and others, there is not much flexibility. There have been significant changes made in the moneys allocated to various departments and agencies,, but there is no budget document that provides us with what the government's thinking is with respect to those changes.
We to your left believe that if the government is going to respect its undertaking to be forthright and to deal in a businesslike manner with the finances of this country, we should have a budget, a clear statement as to what the government intends to do because of the uncertainty. Let us call a spade a spade. Over the next three months, as various individuals seeking the leadership of the Conservative Party go before Canadians, I doubt very much that all will be singing from the same hymn book.
Surely there will be a number of people who will want to distance themselves from the former Minister of Finance who I understand might be a candidate. Who would want to deal with the father of the GST without making some comments about where the country has gone as we have accumulated a debt in excess of $400 billion?
As we get these conflicting statements from various leadership hopefuls, it seems to me that it would be responsible for the government to give a clear and coherent statement to the Canadian people as to how it expects to raise the money that is going to be required to fund the expenditures that we have been made privy to today and how it is going to deal with the deficit that it has talked about for eight years and that is still running at $34 billion. It is talk, talk, talk, but no change in what it is costing Canadians in terms of the year to year increase that is the result of this deficit and the cost of financing our accumulated debt.
In closing, I want to reiterate our belief that it is absolutely essential to maintain the integrity of the
system and the credibility of the system vis-a-vis the Canadian taxpayers that the government bring forth a budget telling us how it wants to deal with the problems facing this country. The government must tell us how it wants to raise the money required to cover these expenditures and how it is going to cover the shortfall between what it can raise and what it plans to spend according to these documents.
We look forward to hearing from members on the government side as to whether they share our view that it might be appropriate to bring a budget before the Canadian people as we lurch along in the fifth year of this government's mandate.

maintopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have in many respects reached a turning point in the life of this government. The Prime Minister has announced his resignation and the government is trying to renew itself. Yet a set of estimates has been presented which in fact demonstrates far too clearly the unfortunate, often I must say, dishonest approach this government has taken toward the public finances of this country.
It is possible however to probe with these estimates below the surface. The government tries to present a surface saying that everything is fine. This morning, people across the country heard the minister say: "We are in fine shape as a country. Everything is starting to move ahead as it should".
Let us look at some of the realities emerging from these estimates. Perhaps the most dramatic are the helicopters which were to cost $4.4 billion according to this government. It turns out in these estimates they will not cost $4.4 billion, but $5.8 billion. That level of extravagance and waste is simply unacceptable in this country.
Moreover, in the fine print of these documents is something which explodes entirely one of the government's major reasons for saying that this helicopter project should go ahead. It suggested that the new EH-101 helicopters would have lower operating costs and this would be a major benefit for Canada. In fact, I quote from part III of the more detailed documents relating to the national defence ministry. It indicates that the annual recurring costs represent "an increment of approximately $33.2 million annually over the combined total of recurring costs of the aircraft fleets which the EH-101 will replace".

Routine Proceedings
In other words, these very helicopters that the government is trying to sell to the Canadian people as being cheaper are going to cost over $33 million more each year. This is the first piece of subterfuge the details of these estimates succeed in exposing.
These estimates also show that we are turning our backs on the poor and the hungry throughout the world. The suggestion was that we might see some cuts in international aid, but I do not think any Canadian realized that the bulk of the cuts that would be established would be in food aid to the poorest people who are starving in this world.
The amounts detailed in these estimates show that food aid directly will be cut by $10.6 million each year and food aid funnelled through other organizations will be cut by $25 million each year. We are talking of a total of over $35 million in cuts to food aid. That food aid would not only help many starving people in this world, but would also help Canadian farmers find outlets for the food they produce. That is what this government is cutting.
There are some other fascinating and sad details in this particular set of estimates. We are looking for national unity in this country. We are looking for economic development and fairness and economic growth across our country. I hate to say that in the details of these estimates there is a serious undercutting and sabotage of the national unity of this country.
In Atlantic Canada grants have been cut for economic development by $19 million. In Ontario, especially northern Ontario these grants have been cut by $1.5 million. In the case of aboriginal economic assistance these grants have been cut by $6 million. In the case of western diversification, development aid for the western provinces, these cuts are $16 million. However, for the province of Quebec there is no cut; there is an increase of $40 million.
We have economic problems throughout this country. For a government to come before this House with a pattern of expenditures that takes away from every part of the country and gives to a single part of the country is not just unfair, it is a devastating attack on our national unity. It is something that should not be permitted. That
is one of the reasons this government must go and go quickly.
As well, there are cuts in this set of detailed expenditure outlines to environmental non-governmental organizations at both the national and international levels. Environmental organizations have been extremely useful and valuable in trying to increase the attention and concern of Canadians with respect to environmental issues.
There are cuts of over $300,000 to environmental organizations here in Canada. There are also cuts to groups such as the Canadian Energy Research Institute which is looking at alternative energy sources. There are cuts to the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada. There are cuts to the chemicals control program of the OECD. There are cuts to the economic commission for Europe's co-operative program to monitor the long range transport of air pollution. These are short-sighted cuts which do not recognize the long-term impact and dangers associated with penny pinching on our environmental concerns for the future.
The reality is this government is spending $5.8 billion on helicopters as compared to the $4.4 billion it said it was spending. If it was not spending that $5.8 billion, if it was not spending more money each year to keep its fleet of helicopters going as a result of the replacement, it would be able to take a more enlightened approach to see that food aid got to the people who need it across this world.
The government would be able to see to it that we had a fair distribution of economic development support throughout this country. It would be able to see to it that environmental programs were supported.
Finally the government would have been able to bring to this House as part of its estimates, as it should have, a set of commitments to support AIDS research which the government has had to indicate in its news release it is not yet in a position to announce. This is much to the distress of AIDS organizations throughout this country. They desperately need the bridge financing to keep programs going to deal with one of the most serious epidemics this country knows.
February 25, 1993

This is a bad set of estimates. I hope this House in committee will reject it.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
We are dealing with a very important subject, the Main Estimates. My point of order is that according to Standing Order 81(4) these estimates being tabled today will be deemed to have been reported to the House by May 31 next. They will be deemed to be reported even though many committees of the House will not have had time to look at the estimates, seriously consider them and possibly pass judgments on the expenditure plan.
The public accounts committee and some members of this House have for many years said that the House should review the presentation of the information given to Parliament that in its present format-there were some 84 volumes tabled this morning-is sometimes indigestible and is not being used by members of Parliament.
If I look at the government's information, it says here: "The estimates document contain a wealth of information regarding the spending plans of the Government of Canada. Though primarily intended for members of Parliament, these documents will prove useful to groups and individuals".
I am not boasting here, but last year for example, the only standing committee that reported in due course was the standing committee that I chair, the public accounts committee. The finance committee, which looks after a lot of very important documents, met once last year to look at estimates. It met once, on April 9, and looked at the estimates for customs and national revenue.
My point is this. Yesterday in this House, I tabled a report dealing with information to Parliament. It was put forth by the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. I would like to put into the record just one paragraph of that report which says-
