speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (for Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-109, an act to amend the Criminal Code, the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act and the Radiocommunication Act be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Departmental envelope.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in support of Bill C-109, as it includes two specific provisions related to privacy which I believe this country needs. The first deals with electronic surveillance and is used by the police. The second is the interception of radio-based telephone communications.
The changes being proposed by my colleague, the Minister of Justice, to part VI and part XV of the Criminal Code respond to a series of Supreme Court decisions which significantly affect the way police and other agents of the state can do their jobs.
The first decision involved an undercover drug investigation. An informant and an undercover police officer rented an apartment which they equipped by placing audio-visual recording equipment within one of the walls. Both the informant and the police officer gave their written consent to the interceptions of their conversations, but the court later held that the interception by the state of private communications without the consent of all of the participants was contrary to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Government Orders
This decision is important because it limits the police in using not only this technique, but also body packs to help undercover agents deal with suspected criminals.
The second case arose out of a suspected gambling operation. A pin-hole video camera was installed in a hotel room. It produced evidence which allowed police to conduct a raid on illegal gambling activities. The court decided that video surveillance and locale, where there was a reasonable expectation of privacy without prior judicial authorization, was also contrary to the charter.
The court also noted that as there is no explicit statutory authority for video surveillance, Parliament should provide for it.
The third case involved the tailing of a suspected serial murderer by using an electronic tracking device installed in the suspect's car. The suspect was eventually charged with blowing up a $2 million communications tower based on evidence collected this way.
The court ruled that an unreasonable search and seizure had occurred because police used the tracking device. However, it also indicated that legislation should be drafted to allow judicial or statutory authority to police to engage in these practices when criminal activities are suspected.
The fourth case arose in a trial for conspiracy to import cocaine. Much of the evidence was based on intercepted private communications obtained by the police after receiving various authorizations. During an appeal, the court held that section 7 of the charter entitled an accused to have access to the material used to obtain an authorization. It noted there was a procedural quagmire to establishing this in an orderly fashion. It called on Parliament to eliminate these difficulties through legislative amendment.
As a result of these four cases and the recommendations made by the courts, the Minister of Justice is proposing the following amendments to the Criminal Code: first to provide for a statutory authority for an electronic lifeline to permit police and others in potentially dangerous situations to have their conversations surreptitiously intercepted by backup teams; second to provide for a warrant procedure for police and others to intercept communications with the consent of a participant to a conversation, to gather evidence or information relevant to suspected criminal activity on reasonable grounds; third, to provide for warrant procedures so the police and other enforcement officials can use video and other surveillance technology such as electronic tracking devices; fourth, to provide protection from civil or criminal liability for individuals assisting in the execution of authorizations or warrants; fifth, to provide for warrants and orders to engage in activities or obtain information or co-operation which would otherwise constitute an unreasonable search or seizure; sixth, to streamline the evidentiary and procedural regime applicable to evidence gathered through electronic surveillance.

The primary purpose of these amendments is to permit the use of technology by police forces in the performance of their duties, but only in a way that does not contravene the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The amendments would have the effect of simplifying the rules of admissibility of evidence. They would also increase the effectiveness of both the police and Crown prosecutors, in accordance with the recommendations of the Supreme Court.
We are talking about the resources police officers need to perform their duties satisfactorily.

The second amendment included in Bill C-109 is close to my own heart and deals with the issue of cellular radios and personal privacy. Not long ago The Financial Post conducted an experiment listening to cellular conversations on an easily obtainable inexpensive scanner. In a brief period of time the Post intercepted calls made by stockbrokers, real estate agents, federal bureaucrats, police and others. The subjects varied from the mundane to the illegal, everything from what to serve for dinner to where to conduct a drug transaction.
The Post gained access to all kinds of confidential information from personal and corporate finances to intimate personal conversations. When you think about it, the potential for damage if scanned information were to be misused is staggering.
February 25, 1993

Government Orders
What might happen to the woman when her car breaks down on a lonely highway and she transmits her location to thousands of eavesdroppers? What could happen to the real estate agent who gives out confidential bidding information over a cellular? What would happen to someone who calls a pizza parlour and gives out his credit card number over a cellular phone?
Although we have all heard stories about public figures caught transmitting sensitive information by cellular, it is ordinary citizens and businesses that are most at risk across this country. During one two-hour session The Edmonton Journal heard one caller give his credit card number over cellular, one woman give her address to a date, several intimate conversations and numerous business telephone calls. Another caller mentioned by name a man recently diagnosed with terminal cancer. It is possible the Journal reporter knew about this before his next of kin.
We know there are hundreds of thousands of people out there with a potential to listen. There are a million Canadians with cellular phones and almost as many with scanners capable of monitoring their calls. Privacy is disappearing and Canadians are worried about it.
I know this for several reasons. The first is that my own department, in concert with several other interested parties from government and industry, has just completed the first comprehensive national survey on privacy.
The results were very interesting and confirmed a few things I had suspected. We found that the majority of Canadians feel they have less privacy today than they had a decade ago. There is a sense that personal privacy is under greater pressure today than used to be the case. We found that Canadians believe new technologies pose increasing threats to personal privacy. Two out of three of the respondents told us that they did not know who to turn to if they wanted to do something about an invasion of their privacy.
Finally, we found out that Canadians hold very strong views that something must be done. While they recognize the need for individual responsibility, they want the government involved either on its own or in partnership with business.

Canadians are worried and they hope their government will do something about this. In fact, I think there is a great deal the government can do.
One of the first things I did when I arrived at the Department of Communications was to ask departmental personnel to look for new ways to deal with protection of privacy in telecommunications. The problem was so new and opinions so diverse that I decided we should first set the ground rules. We had to reach a consensus on what Canadians expect in the way of protection of privacy.
I asked the Department of Communications to draft a set of principles on protection of privacy. We submitted this draft proposal to a committee of informed people representing industry, consumers, the academic world and government for improvements. We then published the results which were submitted to the public last fall. In December, I was able to disclose a set of six principles that those providing telecommunication services are expected to observe.

Briefly, the principles are as follows. Recognition: privacy is a right, respect it. Informed choice: users must be aware of privacy implications of services they are offered. Fairness: where services are introduced which erode personal privacy, privacy should be restored at no charge. Control: personal information should not be used without the customer's permission. The right to be left alone: unsolicited telecommunications must be subject to clear ground rules. Review: as technology in society changes, privacy principles and protection methods should be reviewed.
If these principles had been in place prior to the introduction of cellular services, we might have been able to avoid a lot of grief which has occurred since. A large part of the problem is that people who use cellular radios think they are using telephones, enjoying the same degree of privacy they expect from their regular telephone service.
The truth is a cellular phone is not a telephone at all. Every conversation is a radio broadcast transmitted into the air on radio waves and is very public indeed. Therefore the first part of our strategy has to be public education and we have started that already.

Government Orders
We have also asked my department to release a simple brochure to the public which explains the issues and ways to improve personal privacy. I have also asked cellular service providers to take leadership in informing their customers, ideally through brochures or messages attached to the bills themselves, about the safest way to transmit confidential information. I have also asked my department to work on a media campaign which will help to transmit our message.
The second element is equally important and that is protection. I will ensure that cellular service providers offer effective and affordable encryption services to their customers. I have asked the Communications Research Centre to co-operate with them to help refine and implement these technologies. I am pleased to see that Bell Mobility Cellular has already cut its charges by almost two-thirds.
Encryption alone is not enough. What about the individual who uses a land line and, believing the conversations to be private, receives a call from a cellular? I have asked the Communications Research Centre to explore the technical feasibility of inserting an audible signal on the line which will indicate whenever a cellular is involved.
I am pleased to report we found that there is little to prevent the cellular companies from introducing this new technology.
This brings me to the third crucial element of our strategy which is prosecution. There is nothing particularly damaging about listening into someone else's conversations. However when a third party uses that information or passes it to another party, irreparable damage can take place. Radio-based communications are not specifically addressed in existing legislation because when it was drafted cellulars were not yet on the market. The result is a loophole. Canadians need to have legislative tools to defend themselves against invasions of their privacy. Give them these tools. The Minister of Justice and I are proposing complementary amendments to the Criminal Code and the Radiocommunication Act.
Mr. Speaker, I see that it is almost five o'clock. Perhaps I could pursue this at the next sitting of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
You may or else I will not see the clock. We are anticipating Royal Assent and I am expecting Mr. Speaker to come in very shortly. Maybe the hon. member would like to cany on until Mr. Speaker returns to the Chair.
Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and thanks to my colleagues in the House.
First of all, these amendments will deem all encrypted radio-based telephone communications to be private and protected by the full strength of the law.
Second, the proposed changes to the Criminal Code will prohibit malicious and profit-motivated interception of any radio-based telephone communication. Anyone who deliberately intercepts communications with the intention of harm or any other motive of securing a financial advantage would be subject to prosecution.
Third, with a limited number of exceptions, the disclosure or subsequent use of any intercepted radio-based telephone communication would be prohibited without the consent of a party to it.
Anyone who contravenes these provisions can be punished on summary conviction with a fine of not more than $25,000 and/or one year in jail in the case of an individual, or with a fine not exceeding $75,000 in the case of a corporation.
Finally, the Radiocommunication Act will be amended to allow private right of action. Any victim of such wrongdoing will have the right to take the perpetrator to court for damages. This provision will give a clear civil recourse for individuals who suffer damages because of unauthorized interception.
I am convinced that these provisions for protection, prevention and prosecution, when taken together will offer the most effective solution to the complex issue of privacy.
Not everyone agrees with me. A writer in The Hill Times wrote recently that Bill C-109 was an Orwellian bill which "will stifle everyone's freedom of expression" and that "journalists and all citizens would be vulnerable to prosecution for activities which have never been considered to be immoral or unethical".
February 25, 1993

I do not believe this to be true. If you write something down on a piece of paper and someone else reads it when you have not given them permission, that is considered to be immoral. If someone intercepts your mail, even if it has been sitting untended for hours in your mail box and opens it that is illegal. If you say something on a telephone and someone else uses a wire tap to intercept it they could go to jail. Eavesdropping and using other people's private information has always been considered immoral and unethical. The difference is that technology has outstripped the law and so interception and divul-gence of cellular phone calls for malicious or harmful purposes is not yet considered illegal.
Bill C-109 will protect Canadians by giving them legal recourse if they believe their privacy has been invaded by people who intercept or wilfully disclose a radio-based telecommunication for gain.
The words maliciously and for gain are key. We are not interested in the inadvertent scanner, but the deliberate focused eavesdropper who intends to use other people's private information for his personal gain or for harm.
New technology has promised to speed up and add to the different ways we transfer personal data. It would be irresponsible for the government to ignore this technological revolution and allow open season for anyone wishing to intercept and use information sent this way for their own malicious purposes.
Most people, including journalists, recognize this. As an editorial in the December 12 issue of The Montreal Gazette pointed out: "Had those conversations of Diane Wilhelmy and Bud Smith taken place over conventional phone lines, any authorized person who divulged the contents by tape, transcript or even orally would have been liable to charges. Users of cellular or cordless phones have no such legal protection of privacy".
That is what the federal legislation aims to fix. Clearly, strong measures are needed to discourage scanners from divulging information, blackmail, industrial espionage, credit card fraud or any number of illicit acts.

That in the opinion of this House the government should consider the advisability of substantially increasing federal funds available for job training and retraining programs.

February 25, 1993
Private Members' Business
He said: Madam Speaker, I hope to get a start here before we are summoned to the Senate.
I put a motion before the House today to call upon the federal government to spend more money in terms of training and retraining in this country. I believe it is a very important issue. If we look around our country today, 11 per cent of the work-force is unemployed. Many other people are on social assistance across the country and many more people are working part-time at odd jobs here and there, drawing very low salaries. All that has a tremendous effect on our economy in terms of driving down government revenues, driving up the national debt and driving up the deficit each and every year. Since 1984 the debt in this country under the present government has more than doubled.
One reason for that is we have a very weak economy in Canada. The economy of our country has been going down instead of up and I think we have some long-term structural problems that we have to deal with as a nation. One solution is to spend more money on education, training and retraining of our work-force. Another is to spend more money on research and development.
These are two reasons why our country is not doing as well in many aspects as the Europeans, the Americans to the south of us or the Japanese. We can look at all the statistics and find we are lagging further and further behind.
Years ago theories about labour and capital were important. Today I think knowledge has become the most important thing. Countries that are good in knowledge, information, training, skills and research and development are the countries that will really go ahead.
I would just like to place on the record today a couple of statistics that really paint a very stark picture as to why I moved this motion today. In The Financial Post of March, 1991 I read an article about training and it compared our country to other countries around the world.
In Japan, for example, the average worker gets 200 hours of training per year. In Sweden the average worker receives 170 hours of training per year. In our country the average worker receives 7 hours of training per year.
I think that tells us why we are falling further and further behind.

It is a big problem, because in Canada only seven hours a year per employee are spent on training compared with 170 hours in Sweden and 200 hours in Japan. This means there is a big difference between us, the Europeans and the Japanese.
According to Statistics Canada, the government's own agency for gathering statistics, only 5.3 per cent of Canadian workers in 1987 received any training. If we go to the European countries, to Japan or to the United States, we find that more and more of their workers are receiving training compared with what we have in this country. That is one reason we have tremendous problems of unemployment today.
The other reason is that we are spending less and less on research and development. We are spending less on a per capita base in research and development than the French, the Germans, the Swiss or the Swedes, than indeed most European countries. We are spending much less than the Americans and much much less than the Japanese.
For those kinds of reasons we are falling further behind. I suggest today in my motion that the federal government should start spending more on training and retraining our workers for the challenges that lie ahead.
I believe we have a great country. We have a great future in Canada. We can be second to none in the 21st century. But we are only going to be second to none if we start to make some of the structural changes to be more competitive on a global basis. If we do not do that we will continue to lag behind.
I call on members of the other parties to start doing some thinking about what we can do in terms of putting more money into training. For example, if we look at the private sector we find out that it spends a lot less money training its workers than does the private sector in Europe, Japan or the United States. A lot less money is spent by our corporations, by our business community. It is in their interest to start spending money on training workers in Canada for long-term jobs and in terms of building our economy.
February 25, 1993

When people are working they are paying taxes. When they are paying taxes, the country is stronger and the deficit is lower. We have more money for social programs, more money for economic development, more money to help poor people and more money to help aboriginal people. We have more money to do the things we want in terms of building a strong country.
When people are not working the reverse is true. More people are drawing unemployment insurance. More people are starting to draw welfare across the country or assistance in other forms from the federal and provincial governments. It is not only the federal government that has a fiscal problem. It is now being transferred to the provinces with more and more people being on the welfare rolls.
My province of Saskatchewan is a prime example of that. The unemployment rate for the first time since 1966, when they started keeping statistics on a provincial basis, is 10 per cent despite the fact that it has a net population loss and an aging population. We are in a province that has seen a government debt grow from only $3.5 billion in 1982 to $15 billion today after nine years of Conservative government by Grant Devine.
Yet we see an economy gradually grinding down in comparison to what is happening around the rest of the world because we have not had the foresight at the national level to make ourselves more productive, to spend more money on training and research and development so that we can start producing more things in this country.
There is no reason in the world why we should not be the top-notch people in the world in producing a number of things that are natural to a country like ours. We are the biggest, most vast country in the world. There is no reason we should not be first and foremost in terms of communications and transportation. We have a tremendous resource base. We should be first and foremost in terms of resources, mining machinery, mining equipment and things of that sort. In many cases we are not. We are tremendous agricultural producers in Canada, yet we import a lot of our farm equipment, farm machinery. Research investment dollars in terms of development and technology are spent in other countries around the world. Then we import the technology, the machinery and those devices into Canada.
Royal Assent
These are things that should not be ideological. These are the kinds of things done by governments of the social democratic stripe, Conservative stripe or Liberal stripe in Europe or Japan. These are things that should be done here.
If we were to spend that money it would not be a short-term investment or a short-term cure. It would be a long-term cure. If we were to spend that money today it would pay dividends in five years, ten years and fifteen years down the road. There would be tremendous dividends in terms of dollars and cents and more important dividends in terms of ordinary people on the street who are suffering today, lining up at food banks and unemployment insurance offices or facing the humility of applying for welfare when they have the ability to work and support themselves and their families.
That is the problem. What can we do about it? I suggest two or three things can be done. First, if we had a proper day care system we could start providing more and more children with skills, with a bit more training and education at a very early age. That is something we have talked about in our party for a long time in terms of a national child care policy.
Second, in terms of our schools and universities I get the feeling we are lagging behind many countries in the world as far as teaching our children, our students, the kinds of new skills they need going into the 21st century.
I know it varies from province to province. I have talked to many people who are saying: "We do not think our children are learning what they should in school. They are not getting the kind of information they need compared to what is happening elsewhere". This is something that is under provincial jurisdiction, but once we get to the universities it is the federal government that pays much of the bill.
I hear a knock at the door. After royal assent I will continue with my remarks.

Madam Speaker, I will be very brief because my friend from St. John's East is champing at the bit. He wants to make a long speech and announce what a wonderful motion this is. My motion is to spend more money on training and retraining in this country.
An excellent idea.

It is a very good idea in terms of what we should be doing. We call it an investment, investing in our future.
I have already suggested we should do more in our educational system; in our schools, our universities. I believe the private sector has to do a lot more.
One thing we suggested in a recent document, our job strategy, is to phase in a 2 per cent levy on corporations and businesses that have more than 10 employees. If that were done we could raise, on a 2 per cent levy on their payroll, about a $7 billion fund for training and retraining. We believe that could be phased in over a number of
years and would be an investment in the future of Canada.
Firms that were already doing training in their own right would not have a levy imposed on them. Those that did not have their own training programs would pay into a fund where there would be training programs set up on behalf of the country in general. These are some of the things that could be done.
The other thing that could be done is the federal government itself could spend more money on training, retraining and research and development in the country. Those are some of the things that should be done.
I wanted to move this motion today to try to move the debate along. It is important to look at long-term solutions to the problems we have in this country. These are some of the things which will solve some of the problems that we face in restructuring our economy, making it more competitive, putting more people to work and allowing more people to make a contribution. If we do that I think we have a tremendous future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak on this motion from my very good friend from Yorkton-Melville who, as quite often is the case in this place, makes some very good sense.
The essence of the motion and the comments that we have just heard is that the commitment to training in this country is something that we must recognize as an investment, partly in our present but more particularly in our future. It is a responsibility all of us share. It is a benefit that in the long run all of us will share. A country whose work force is trained has a capacity to take on more knowledge and more training, is a work force that is adaptable, that is flexible and can modernize itself as the demands of the economy dictate and change.
To my mind one of the unfortunate conditions of education and training in this country today is that we do not see education as a life-long process. The attitude of many of us is that we go to school, graduate from an institute of secondary education and then many of us, who have been lucky enough, go on to post-secondary education but that is it.
My friend talks about the fact that the private sector spends so little compared to other countries. That is quite true. Every dollar that the private sector spends on
February 25, 1993

training-I think it is $2 in the United States, $5 in Japan, and in Germany about $8-says an awful lot not only about the attitude of our economy but the attitude of this country toward education and training.
There are a number of comments that come to mind in that area. I have long been very concerned about our attitude in the comparison of an academic education to a technical education. Far too many of us, be we legislators or public servants or educators or students, often give less value to a non-academic education. It is a loss, it is a tragedy and it is unfair and based on nothing. I would suggest it is an attitude we must overcome as we face a very technical world and a world of very great challenge in terms of our capacity not only to deal with technology but to manufacture and process technology.
The question is, should we be spending more? Yes, we should be spending more and continue to spend more.
In 1992-93 Employment and Immigration Canada is investing $3.55 billion in training for over 900,000 Canadians. Next year Employment and Immigration Canada will spend about $3.8 billion in training for over one million Canadians.
What is it spent on? There are a number of programs I can talk about: $110 million for self-employment assistance; skills training for 326,000 Canadians, 164,000 of those are courses purchased by Employment and Immigration Canada for $430 million; another 162,000 will arrange their own training under the fee payer program; $120 million budgeted for job creation under the unemployment insurance job creation program where 31,000 unemployed workers will get back and $130 million for the work-sharing assistance program.
I want to take the opportunity to comment on a couple of things that are happening in my constituency and province. I am told that one of the highest expenditures by a constituency on training in this country is in St. John's East. Frankly that is not as much a testimonial to my ability to get funds as it is to the academic institutions in my community and constituency and the number of community groups that have come forward and said that
Private Members' Business
they have a contribution to make in the training of others.
Memorial University is recognized as one of the best medium-sized universities in this country, with a whole variety of very specialized and very important international faculties. The Cabot Institute or Cabot College was what we used to call a trade school and is now a technical institution in my constituency. It has a number of campuses: three in St. John's, one on Belle Island which is in Conception Bay and one in Seal Cove. They are important contributors to the community. They are providers of education. They are sources of innovation.
We are telling young people that the education they get not only helps them take advantage of opportunities and creates opportunities in the future, but the process of education and training is in and of itself valuable. It gives the opportunity not only to learn from books but to see the world from a different focus and a different function.
I want to very quickly mention the business school at Cabot where they have tried to take practical opportunities to learn about trade in terms of what Newfoundland and Labrador businesses are doing in pursuing their opportunities and exposing their students to them. The initiative of the faculty, such as Dan Mosher and Dean Baker and others, to ask government and companies if they could take these students and expose them to opportunities that they may see for the future, gives their training more relevance and more practical application.
We are aware of the Pathways to Success program which is important for aboriginal people. I want to refer to a couple of others that have been particularly important. We have two WISE programs. One is Women Interested in Successful Employment and one is Women Interested in Science and Engineering. They have very different focuses and functions. One is very much a grassroots community program that is I think sponsored under the job entry component of the Canadian Jobs Strategy. It provides women who have been out of the education milieu and out of the work force for a considerable period of time not only the tools and skills

February 25, 1993
Private Members' Business
to get back into the work force or into the work force for the first time, but self-confidence.
People ask why we are spending all this money on self-confidence. I have never seen anything like the transformation those women go through having completed those courses, and the contribution they make not only to their families and their communities but to the economy of which they now want to become a part.
Women Interested in Science and Engineering and another program known as Wi l l are designed to expose women to science, engineering and also the technical opportunities that developments like Hibernia provide. They are driven by the recognition that not only non-traditional occupations should be pursued but also that women particularly have the capacity, the capability, an interest and a desire to pursue them. They not only should be looking at non-traditional occupations for women but women want to be able to develop a knowledge of technology and an exposure to technology to open up all sorts of new vistas.
I think that approach of putting the academic community together with the business community together with two levels of government and going forward in partnership is providing training opportunities the likes of which we have never seen before.
I can mention numerous other projects that have been developed to provide skill training, to enhance the training that people have or to bring job opportunities to allow the skills that are already in possession to be able to be maintained as job opportunities come along.
One of the biggest components of the fisheries program for which we in this country will spend approaching $1 billion is saying to those people that through the moratorium are either not fishing or not working in fish plants that they will have the opportunity for training either inside or outside the fishery.
The work of the Fishermen Food and Allied Workers Union in developing these training programs under the directorship of Father Des McGrath will prove that while people have not been working, they have been taking advantage of the opportunities provided through these programs.
As we deal with the opportunities of oil and gas, hands-on training, specific skills reinforced with basic skills training is a particularly critical component.
If there is any approach that we need to take as we go into the 21st century as my friend says, it is to have the basic capacity to continue training and education. It is that life-long process of training and education that we must adopt in this country if we are going to have the flexibility to take advantage of the opportunities of the next century.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate because I am a firm believer that training is indeed important in establishing this country as a leader in the 21st century. I believe that training is crucial to young people who need it to succeed in the global marketplace and it is important for older workers who must adapt to our changing economy.
As we all know, our economy is going through a period of profound transformation. While in the past we were able to rely on our abundant natural resources to pay for our standard of living, that is no longer the case. Many of our forefathers could expect to get work in the forestry, fishery or mining industries and have a good job for life. Others could look forward to long careers working at an automobile plant, a textile factory or a steel mill. That kind of job security is a thing of the past. The era of well paying, low skills jobs has ended for Canada.
In order to compete against Germany, Japan and the United States, not to mention South Korea, Taiwan and Mexico, Canada must focus on creating a high skills, high wage economy. Tb do that we must invest in training.
As we move from a resource based economy to a knowledge based economy, we must help Canadians acquire the skills they need to prosper in the new global marketplace. The fact is that training is not a luxury, it is a prerequisite for prosperity in the 21st century and beyond.
Throughout its term in office I have called on the government to increase its commitment to training in recognition of that fact. Unfortunately, the government does not seem to realize how urgent the question is. While it talks a great deal about the establishment of a
February 25, 1993

learning culture, the present government does not reinforce its words with actions.
For example, on February 7, 1992, the minister of employment said in this House: "This government has shifted the priority from make-work projects to training in order to help young Canadians obtain jobs that can last". That is simply not the case. The fact is that while the government has shifted funds in order to train UI recipients, it has consistently cut the amount it spends on training for Canadians who do not receive UI.
Last year the government cut $200 million from its general training budget. Gerald Docquier, co-chair of the Canadian Labour Force Development Board called those cuts devastating. He also said that increases in training funds from the UI fund should not absolve the government of its responsibility to ensure that Canada has a well trained work force.
This is because most Canadians do not have access to training funds earmarked for UI recipients. Many students graduate from university and cannot find work. They are ineligible for training programs funded through unemployment insurance. Many women, immigrants, disabled Canadians and aboriginal Canadians do not have access to these training funds.
People who have exhausted their UI benefits, and there are many in this situation after a three year recession, cannot apply for these training programs.
A case was recently brought to my attention where a training advisory board has money for training but cannot spend it because the money has been allocated for UI recipients and all the people who might benefit from these training programs have exhausted their UI benefits. That is unbelievably sad.
At a time when so many Canadians need training in order to find work, it is unacceptable that people are excluded because of the neglect this government has demonstrated on the training issue.
We in the Liberal Party understand that if the government does not get serious about training, Canada is going to be left behind by our foreign competitors.
Private Members' Business
Liberals understand that without a real commitment to training, we cannot hope to help the 460,000 people whose jobs disappeared in the recession. Liberals understand that without a commitment to training we cannot promise a future to our young people.
As a member of Parliament, I have spent the last four years listening to the voices of young people throughout Canada. Many young people are worried about their prospects. Many have lost hope and have given up on the possibility of ever finding a rewarding career.
As co-chair of the Liberal Senate and House of Commons committee on youth, I was pleased to present a number of recommendations on training to our party. In a major policy speech on January 27 our leader outlined what a Liberal government would do in this area.
He said that a Liberal government would work in partnership with business, labour, educational institutions and other governments to create a national apprenticeship program. He also said that a Liberal government would put in place a tax based incentive to encourage on-the-job training.
Another aspect of our program for young people would be the establishment of a Canadian youth service to help young people develop the skills and work habits that are much required in a competitive society.
A Liberal government would take these steps because we understand the importance of training. We understand that we cannot afford to waste 100,000 high school students who drop out of high school each year.
Anyone who questions whether or not the government should be doing more in this area should remember these two figures: First, there are 1.6 million Canadians who cannot find work. Second, there are approximately
600,000	good jobs that cannot be filled because we lack people with the skills needed to fill them.
Those numbers reflect a great injustice toward the unemployed. The government has a responsibility to address that injustice and see that unemployed Canadians find work. The best way and the only way to help these people is through training.

Private Members' Business
Therefore, I call on the government to take immediate action and address the urgent training needs of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I would first like to congratulate the youth critic for the Liberal Party for having noticed some of the recommendations that the New Democratic task force on youth wrote in the year 1985.
He might expand upon that and perhaps study the proposition of a youth opportunity program that would show no bias among choices with respect to colleges or universities or with respect to training or entrepreneurship. He would be aware of our recommendations with respect to work experience, co-operative programs and all levels of education.
He would know something about the grant levy proposal for training in industry which was a part of that document. It is a part of the document that the New Democratic Party released last week with respect to the creation of jobs in this country based on a solid economic plan in order to accomplish that.
I would like to congratulate the Liberals for reviewing history and catching up with it. They have not yet achieved the detailed proposals for actually doing something about attacking the inadequacy of opportunities for lifelong learning not only for youth but for all Canadians.
I found the discussion that was introduced by my colleague up until this point a very edifying one, but I think there is still a tendency to have a relatively narrow perspective. I agree with the hon. member when he says that the global economy has changed substantially and that the focus in the new economies is on knowledge, skills and learning. For this country to compete, it is obvious that we must enhance the opportunities for training and education at all levels so we can be more competitive.
However, I think that our analysis has so far been based on a rather narrow construction of what is really at issue here. Not only does a new global economy require a higher skill level to achieve higher wages and increase higher value added, it implies an absolutely different structure and organization of the work place.
No longer, as the hon. member mentioned, are we going to have a situation in which workers can depend upon access to jobs which are dependent upon a routine, standardized, low knowledge based assembly line process in which management gave commands to the workers and where there was a strict hierarchical structure. Instead there would be a work place in which the success of a corporation, the successful production of goods and services is going to depend upon a great deal of mutual respect for the particular skills and knowledge that every worker, described as management or otherwise, is going to be a precious, necessary thing. It means that the status of the worker is going to improve in terms of his or her contribution.
In other words, I am trying to say that the worker of the new economy is going to be an empowered worker. It will be someone who has the confidence that he or she has something to contribute that everyone else in the work place is bound to respect because he or she has it.
That is why the New Democratic job strategy, although described as an attempt to deal with the deficit and all of those things is, in fact, a strategy for the empowerment of the Canadian people.
The hon. member for St. John's East alluded to this empowerment when he described the reaction of women who had an opportunity to gain more training. If we have missed the point, the New Democratic job strategy is focused on empowering the people through skills and knowledge and it recognizes that for all we may say about improving training and all we may say about lifelong learning, we have not yet got to the core of the problem.
In the new global economy, if there is one thing that we as government can affect in a significant way, it is the capacity of our work force to contribute to the creation of wealth, the prospect that the workers will be empowered economically, socially and politically because that new worker empowered by education and training is not going to be the worker who is going to take the guff of the sort this government has handed down any more than the guff employers too often impose on workers. But then the employer of the future will also be a very different employer, one who recognizes that inherent quality of the work force which can, through its creativity, knowledge and capacity, create wealth and success for this country.
February 25, 1993

We must start at the very beginning. We talk about those who are being trained through UI and through the Canada Jobs Strategy, but what is being ignored is the 35 per cent of the population who still remain functionally illiterate. Any program to address the issue of training and education that does not include an urgent attack on that level of illiteracy will fail the country, fail our prospects and fail the many people of this country.
We cannot miss the fact that there is a changed social environment in which many children are confronted with the reality that in their lifetime 65 per cent of them will sooner or later have a single parent struggling to raise them and if they have both parents in most situations both of them will be working. So the kind of educational preparation that we can usually assume is going to exist in a home and which has been traditional in the past can no longer exist.
We talk about investing $2 billion in day care. Yes, that is to the benefit of parents, but fundamentally it is aimed at starting at the very base of the issue by providing every kid in this country with the kind of educational preparation that will be necessary to succeed in the schools of the future.
Yes, it is true we spend more on education than virtually any other industrial nation. However, it must be clear that it requires dramatic reform and national leadership if our educational policies are going to be in accord with the economic future we intend to achieve for this country.
My hon. colleague has brought forward a motion that we should all support, which is that there needs to be more investment in training and retraining. In our job strategy we propose a grant levy tax system on industry so that industry that does not train its workers would be taxed and industry that does train will not be taxed.
Mr. Speaker, I only have 10 minutes. I can see that you are waving your hands and saying: "I know that you should go on, but the time limits do not permit you to do so". However the substance of it is that if we are going to develop as a successful economic player in this new world global economy it is not going to be by talking about resources as human resources or any of this sort. It has to be based on-
Private Members' Business

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I love to hear the hon. member in debate, but I must cut him off. It has been a little over 10 minutes now.

Mr. Speaker, I shall attempt to say as much in 2 minutes as my colleague has in more than 10 minutes.
It would appear to me that the first thing we must come to grips with when we talk about education, training and retraining is a sense of vision of where the country is headed. We must know exactly what it is that we want this nation, Canada, to become and know the kinds of relationships, trade and others, that we are going to undertake with other nations.
It is only logical that it is only then that we can address two basic questions. What do we need in terms of education, training, retraining, and research and development, to continue to provide those individuals who will make sure what we have working in our country today will continue to happen? We have people who will be taking retirements and people who will be going to other jobs so we need a certain group of workers to make sure that what is happening today will continue.
We need to address another question that is much more difficult. What are those new jobs of the future? Those jobs of the future can only be determined if we know where we are going as a nation, if we understand the kinds of relationships that we are going to have with our trading partners and if we have insights into what will happen. Otherwise, we are educating and training in a void.
I would also like to suggest that we need appropriate support for colleges and universities. That absolutely must be a priority. We also need an enhanced apprenticeship program.
I am delighted that my leader has made that a priority. We need to focus on the importance of learning in the work place. Learning in the work place is an area that has been underestimated and has not been sufficiently appreciated.
We also need to make awfully certain that there is a better co-ordination of the relationships between the learning institutions and the work place. This is of critical importance.

February 25, 1993
Adjournment Debate
Finally, I believe that we have not appropriately understood the importance of having programs to respond to the needs of older workers. Retraining them will be a major priority in the future because, as a number of my colleagues have said, learning is going to be a lifetime undertaking.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask again the question that I asked the Minister of Agriculture on November 26, 1992 regarding the changes being pushed by this government in terms of the method of payment of the Crow benefit to the railways, and the removal of barley exports to the United States from under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board.
The background to this question is that the net worth of Saskatchewan farmers has fallen $8 billion since this government was elected in 1984. The average projected family income of Saskatchewan farmers next year is going to be $4,000, which is less than they would make on welfare. It is also a startling statistic that there are more farmers in Saskatchewan over 70 than under 30.
It is against this backdrop that the government is pushing changes to the Crow benefit, which would change the method of payment from the railways, where it has historically been paid, to the producers.
As well, since the time I asked this question the government has made a 10 per cent cut in that Crow benefit, which in my constituency alone represents a drop of more than one million dollars in income to
farmers and in the money they have to spend with businesses there.
Why is the minister pressing ahead with these changes when it will have an impact on the value of farmland, cause a drop in farm income and further unravel the social and physical infrastructure of prairie Canada? Why is he pressing ahead with these changes when over 70 per cent of Saskatchewan farmers said they did not want them and when the one thing that the 13,000 farmers at the farm rally in Saskatoon on January 26 were unanimous about was that they did not want changes in the Crow rate?
Second, why is the minister proposing to take barley exports out of the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board when his own figures indicate that since the government has taken oats from under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board, exports of oats to the United States have been cut in half while the export of grains that have been controlled by the Canadian Wheat Board has virtually doubled in that period of time?
Why is the Minister of Agriculture continuing to treat agriculture like the black knight in the Monty Python movie by lopping off one limb at a time until finally agriculture is left dancing around on bloody stumps not able to get anywhere?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must indeed give the hon. member credit for presenting his argument in a colourful fashion. However I regret to say that the basis on which the argument is made is not well founded.
In fact, the Government of Canada has not proposed to change the method of payment nor has it proposed to take the sale of continental barley out of the control of the Canadian Wheat Board.
The Government of Canada has addressed these two important issues as ones which require further study, consultation with producers, and consultation with the industry in general. That consultation is now under way.
We provide some $700 million annually to the grain industry to assist with the costs of movement of grain to export points. The question is how to most efficiently use that $700 million or so. That is the issue that is being discussed, and it is being discussed in consultation with all the players.
With respect to the question of the method of sales of barley to the continental United States market, I want to stress that the discussion and study which is now taking
February 25, 1993

place relates only to that portion of barley sales, and that it is a consultation which has taken place. Unfortunately, the hon. member is very wrong when he implies that there is a set government position because that is just not the case.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have come here this evening to speak on a subject which is of great concern to my constituency, namely unemployment.
On February 19, 1993 I posed a question to the government with regard to the consequential effects of a bill it introduced with amendments to unemployment insurance. At that time I asked what these changes to the unemployment insurance would do for the people of my constituency.
We have an unemployment rate of 26.4 per cent. That is the last recording we have from Statistics Canada. My constituents in Glace Bay, New Waterford, Reserve, Gardiner, Dominion, Louisbourg, Sydney River, Mira Road, South Bar, Grand Lake Road, L'Ardoise, Framboise, East Bay, Ben Eoin and all other parts of Richmond county as well as Cape Breton county are feeling the effects of the government's actions and inactions over the last number of years.
I would hope that the parliamentary secretary who will respond on behalf of the government will understand that these regressive measures, as contained in the piece of legislation making changes to the unemployment insurance, will do absolutely nothing for those individuals who find themselves without work or, worse still, who find themselves having to go to municipal and provincial welfare.
As I have said repeatedly in this Chamber through you, Mr. Speaker, to hon. members opposite, my constituents do not wish to be on unemployment insurance. They do not wish to be on municipal or provincial social assistance. They wish to have the opportunity to have a meaningful job. I suggest that this government has been grossly negligent in bringing forward policies which would have a positive effect on the Canadian economy, in particular the regional economies of this country.
Adjournment Debate
I find it unsatisfactory that the Minister of National Defence would proceed with the program of putting billions of dollars into helicopters when in fact we have such high unemployment in the areas I have just previously mentioned. It is not fair. It is wrong. It is stupid. It is idiotic. It represents a government which has lost touch with the ordinary Canadian.
I have come forward tonight to speak on their behalf, to get the opportunities and jobs so they can provide for their families and make a contribution to the society we all hope they want.
In conclusion, I urge the parliamentary secretary to stand in his place and tell the people of my district what these unemployment insurance changes are going to mean for them and how he will create the kinds of jobs we need in the great district of Cape Breton-East Richmond.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration of Canada, I am pleased to inform the hon. member that the government is fully aware of the economic difficulties in certain regions of the country including Cape Breton.
EIC offers a wide range of programs and services to all Canadians, the unemployed, the employed, the underemployed, employers, and communities. The type of assistance offered depends on a number of factors such as what type of assistance is needed. Sometimes this means counselling or a service needs determination test. It may mean one of our training programs.
We have recently streamlined all of our services into four programs. This was done so that we could better serve our clients. These programs in the 1992-1993 budget are as follows: information and special initiatives for all clients, $43 million; employability improvement for worker clients, $865 million; community development for communities, $122 million; labour market adjustment for employer clients, $273 million. We believe these four programs make up an effective way to help Canadians find and keep meaningful employment.
I can assure the hon. member that Cape Breton has and will continue to receive its fair share of funding. Last year Employment and Immigration Canada through the Canadian Jobs Strategy provided Cape Breton with over $32 million.

February 25, 1993
Adjournment Debate
There are now several programs and committees in place to deal with the situation in Cape Breton. For example, the community initiatives fund, community futures committees, business development centres, and industrial adjustment services agreements are in place.
I see my time is running out. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the hon. member for his concern.

Mr. Speaker, last week I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare specifically to explain how the department's new health policy to hand over the administration of non-insured health services of First Nations people to Blue Cross, a private corporation, would further the cause of self-government.
I did not think his answer was satisfactory so I would like to raise the issue again. The minister stated that the process of implementing this new policy had been done normally. The appropriate consultations, he said, had taken place and despite the resistance in Manitoba the phasing in of this new policy would continue.
I do not believe the minister fully understands or is listening to the position taken by the First Nations people of Manitoba.
Simply stated the First Nations people of Manitoba strongly object to the unilateral redefining of their health services by the federal government. The minister must realize and accept that it is a long time historical and traditional belief by elders and all First Nations people that quality health care services and non-insured health benefits are a treaty right.
First Nations people have asserted this right since treaties were first signed with the Crown in 1870. The federal government believes health services are provided only as a matter of policy. Why then will it not provide an explanation for this position? Why will it not enter into nation-to-nation dialogue to examine the assertion that health services are a treaty right?
It is constitutionally, legally and morally wrong for the federal government to make unilateral changes to health services without the agreement of the First Nations.
Is the minister aware the Supreme Court has ruled the federal government may not modify policy which impacts
on treaty rights without first seeking the concurrence of First Nations? Why does the minister and his government speak of the right to self-government but act differently? The contract for non-insured native health services was given to Blue Cross by selected tender. Why were First Nations not offered a chance to bid?
In giving the contract to a non-native corporation the government is taking away from First Nations people the opportunity for employment, decision making, accountability and self-determination.
Administering this new program will provide employment opportunities. First Nations communities experience 90 per cent unemployment. Of the 125 employees employed by Blue Cross in Manitoba two people, 1.5 per cent, are aboriginal.
The minister believes that the Blue Cross administration will better serve aboriginal people in Canada. Surely then he must admit that this new policy is not without its own shortcomings. How can he unilaterally determine what is best for aboriginal people without having their full support and participation in any decision-making process? He has also stated that his department will continue in collaboration with aboriginal people.
In closing I ask the minister to consider that a number of Manitoba First Nations and tribal councils have willingly put together plans for managing this package of non-insured health benefits. This would be self-government in action. He should make public to the First Nations people of Manitoba, as they have repeatedly asked, the Manitoba Blue Cross contract document. Why is the federal government holding back?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, non-insured health benefits or health services are provided to registered Indians and Inuit in Canada by the medical services branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Some services include the provision of prescription drugs, medical supplies and equipment, transportation for medical reasons, vision care services such as eyeglasses, and dental care. The non-insured health benefits program is designed to help registered Indians and Inuit reach a level of health comparable to that of other Canadians.
February 25, 1993

Adjournment Debate
Non-insured health benefits of various types have been paid for and provided to registered Indians and Inuit by the federal government for many years. In 1979 a variety of policies, practices and guidelines were replaced with a new Indian health policy. This was based on three principles of community development, the traditional relationship of the Indian people to the federal government and the utilization of the existing Canadian health system.
Since 1979 national non-insured health benefit program expenditures have increased from $36 million to over $400 million in 1992-93. Eligible beneficiaries have increased from 325,000 registered Indians and Inuit in 1979 to 560,000 in 1992.
Because of criticisms about the lack of adequate management and control of non-insured health benefits programs, Health and Welfare Canada was asked by Treasury Board and the Auditor General to make concerted efforts to implement administrative improvements.
This has been accomplished by the development of directives and administrative procedures coupled with the development and implementation of a health information and claims processing system under a contract with Ontario Blue Cross.
First Nations were informed of the changes and officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare met on numerous occasions to describe the changes and inform First Nations leaders and communities of the program. Workshops have been held in many regions at regional, tribal and community levels.
The Manitoba First Nation leaders have taken the position that the directives are an attempt by the federal government to define treaty rights unilaterally. Manitoba chiefs have also claimed that implementation of the automated claims processing system by Blue Cross is a move to transfer federal responsibility to the private sector.
The position of the federal government is that the program is derived from the Indian health policy and changes to it in no way prejudice or are intended to prejudice treaty rights. The federal government retains full control of the non-insured health benefits program and Blue Cross is merely providing administrative support for an automated system to process claims and provide information on benefits utilization.
The system is operating and functioning well in Ontario, Saskatchewan and Quebec. Health and Welfare Canada did not have the capacity to operate the automated process and pay the bills. It decided to identify a company with the capacity to develop and operate the system through the normal Supply and Services Canada tendering process. Open tender was called from the companies with experience in the area of health insurance. A significant number of companies indicated interest and attended the bidders conference. Four of those companies or groups submitted tenders from which the successful bidder was picked. Blue Cross was the successful bidder.
Health and Welfare Canada is committed to self-government and has approached First Nations leaders to discuss the development of a framework with which non-insured health benefits can be considered for transfer. One of the prerequisites of central agencies prior to approval being given to the transfer of this program is that the costs should be within control.
The automated system allows the department to demonstrate the real costs of the program. This information allows for accurate forecasting expenditures and the development of a formula or formulae for allocations upon transfer.
As soon as these parameters are developed and agreed upon, transfer authority will be sought.

Mr. Speaker, I rise as a follow-up to a question I raised with the Minister of National Defence on February 16. It concerned peacekeeping.
The tenor of the question was based on the concern and observation that there are a number of red flags being thrown up regarding the manner in which we deploy our troops, the risk that is under way and the strain on personnel resources and operational maintenance resources for the remainder of the Canadian forces. The fact that these operations take place without consideration in Parliament I believe is the overriding concern.
Another reason for the concern and the real reason I am here tonight is that I see the Canadian forces participating in peacekeeping operations because of their excellent record in this regard and because of the understandable desire of any government, including our own, to participate and continue to participate given the condition of the world today.

February 25, 1993
Adjournment Debate
There is a point when I believe discretion has to be used. Peacekeeping in the last four years has more than doubled. In fact more peacekeeping operations have taken place or been generated in the last four years than in the past forty and I do not see that decreasing. I will tell you why. There are 179 countries in the world today speaking 4,000 languages. I think 60 of them have a population of one million or less and 40 of them have a population of less than 200,000. More importantly, less than 10 per cent of these countries have a homogeneous ethnic population and less than 5 per cent have an ethnic group that accounts for more than 75 per cent of the population.
Therefore what you are in fact seeing is an explosion of nation states downward to the point where they are really comprising the smallest ethnic or religious groups.
In fact it is tribalism. These forces of tribalism and nationalism are intractable forces. I think you are going to see more and more of it as time goes by.
If you add to that the low level of tolerance that seems to be dominant in the world today for religious, social and ethnic differences, then I think that is another nail in the coffin for more peacekeeping operations.
I should really call them peace operations because, Mr. Speaker, as you are well aware, the United Nations is now responding to peace operations in many ways, not just peacekeeping in its traditional sense as we know in the Cyprus operation in which we have been involved for many years.
There are things like humanitarian assistance as we have in Somalia, guarding food convoys as we have in Bosnia and indeed such things as election monitoring as we have in Cambodia. None of these operations, despite the heroic efforts of the men and women in the field, appear to be moving with a great deal of success. That is another reason why we have concerns.
I merely want to follow up on the minister's response which touched on the business of some time in the future being discretionary only because we will have run out of resources. I trust that my remarks will have some influence on the minister and indeed on the government
as they make future decisions on committing our forces to peacekeeping operations.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to be able to reply on behalf of the hon. Minister of National Defence, particularly to my hon. friend from Bonavista-Trinity-Conception. You may not know this, Mr. Speaker, but our ridings are side by side at least for one patch of about 30 kilometres.
The point that my colleague makes is one that I guess should have been obvious to many of us over time. It is one that is only becoming evident now as Canada continues, by the force of its tremendous reputation, its tremendous commitment and tremendous quality of her forces to be asked to participate in the variety of operations that my colleague referred to earlier.
The point he makes that should have become evident and is now very much becoming evident is that it cannot go on forever. Canada cannot be everywhere all the time. That I think is clearly understood in a number of ways by national defence.
For instance, in Somalia, while we are part of the enforcement action, we have made it clear to the United Nations that we are not going to be able to be part of the subsequent UNOSOM II process. These are decisions one has to make.
It is clear that each operation must be evaluated not only in terms of risk but in terms of personnel, equipment availability and duration. For Canada to assess its position in any United Nations operation, it must be assessed in light of that capacity and also the impact that it has on the ongoing numbers and responsibility of the Canadian forces.
Another response involves obviously the ability of Canada to be more creative in the approaches it takes in meeting these responsibilities in these calls.
The minister while appearing at committee the other day said something and I will not go through the whole quote. She said:
We are looking at a number of new ideas on how to participate in
future peacekeeping operations.
February 25, 1993

One emphasis she would put is perhaps on our skills within our forces as opposed to simply people. The effort that we have made in developing the capacity of our reserves is particularly important. Our troops are very well trained. They are very well prepared. When the reservists are sent into these situations, they receive the same 90-day course that our regular forces receive.
There are 460 reserve peacekeepers serving on United Nations missions at present. They are constituents of mine as I know they are constituents of my friend across the way.
We must have a flexible general purpose combat capable armed force. The number of the reservists in our forces makes that possible. They have a number of roles to play.
It is critical that the Department of National Defence reinforce that with funding. That is important. I know my friend, even though his experience is on the sea, will appreciate that the land forces component of national defence will see a 12.3 per cent increase in expenditures over the last fiscal year.
Mr. Speaker, I see you giving the message that my time is up. I commend my colleague for raising a point that is important. I hope I have been able to shed some light on it. I certainly appreciate your endurance this afternoon as I go on far beyond my time, as is quite often the case.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the day after the Minister of Finance tabled his economic statement last December I rose in the House and asked the Minister of State for the Environment what the impact of that particular statement by the minister would be on the government's green plan, be it the number of programs that are involved with that, the Fraser River basin management plan, model forests and other particular programs. I asked that of the government because it was, as many people said then, a black day for the green plan.
We have seen further in the estimates today a new way of cutting funds. It is called reprofiling of funds for some very important programs.
Adjournment Debate
I hope that tonight the parliamentary secretary can respond and shed some light on the nature of the funding of the green plan because I think it is fair to say that for many who have been following the plan, it has been very difficult to determine department by department, with the profiling or the reprofiling by the government of the funds in the green plan, where we actually are at when it comes to the funding under the program.
I note under the estimates that were tabled today in the House that the government is intending to release a progress report on the green plan in April. I would encourage the government, through the parliamentary secretary, to make a very clear outline of just exactly where we are going with the funding under this particular program.
It is very important to the country that we know what is happening with the green plan and many of the projects under that taking place in our ridings. I referred previously to the Fraser River program in my area. There is a model forests program taking place there as well.
I would ask the parliamentary secretary if he could address some of those comments and certainly take it to the minister. When this progress report is released, let us have some progress, let us have some light shed on just what kind of spending plans there are by this government for the green plan.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree with my hon. friend when he talks about the importance of the green plan. As you know very well, Mr. Speaker, this indeed is the first long-term comprehensive environmental protection program put forth in Canada by any government. In fact, not only is it a first in Canada, but indeed it is a first throughout much of the world.
That is one of the reasons why Dr. Mostafa Iblba, who was director of UNEP prior to Elizabeth Dowdeswell, was so supportive of it.
On the other hand, the Government of Canada is facing some very harsh economic realities based upon the fact that we have a national debt which exceeds $400 billion. We have annual deficits running in the $30 billion range due to the excessive expenditures which occurred at an earlier time and under different circumstances.
*

February 25, 1993
Adjournment Debate
I want to stress today, and I think my hon. friend is probably aware of it, that while most departments in the federal government are either experiencing a freeze or in some cases even having to accept a reduction in the amounts available to them, the amount of money available under the green plan has actually been increasing on a year-by-year basis.
For example, the Main Estimates for 1993-94 total $351 million which, according to my calculations, is a 23 per cent increase from 1992-93. That is a very significant increase. Indeed, it demonstrates that the principal objectives of the green plan will clearly be met, albeit over a greater extended period of time than originally anticipated.
I think it is important for us to remember that the green plan is about a lot of things other than just spending. I think one of the dangers quite frankly is we tend to measure government programs only in terms of dollars spent. I think that is a false premise on which to evaluate.
The green plan is about decision making. The green plan therefore is about our ratification of the Convention on Biodiversity where we provided such leadership at Rio.
The green plan is about the Environmental Assessment Act that has been proclaimed into law and will soon be implemented.
The green plan is about the fact that the North American free trade agreement itself was subjected to environmental assessment, the first such major policy initiative so subjected in Canada.
It is about pulp and paper regulations which are very important in your province, Mr. Speaker. It is about a code of environmental stewardship.
Mr. Speaker, if you would give me additional time, which I know you cannot do under the rules, we would have a greater opportunity to discuss how this plan is so significant to decision making.
We must remember that the green plan is more than just spending. It is how decisions are made. That will be the ultimate value of the green plan in years to come. [Translation]
